stem: A patient who is a known case of arthritis presents with acute abdominal pain and pneumoperitoneum on imaging. What is the most likely cause?
srcNote: The original X-ray shown here is from the merged Midterm 434 Q57 recall.
expl: A patient with arthritis takes NSAIDs (± steroids) — the classic cause of peptic ulcer. Sudden acute abdominal pain with pneumoperitoneum (free air) = perforated hollow viscus, most often a perforated peptic ulcer.

why.A: Small bowel obstruction gives dilated loops and air-fluid levels, not free air (unless it perforates late).
why.B: Correct — NSAIDs → ulcer → perforation → free air.
why.C: A ruptured ectopic pregnancy causes haemoperitoneum, not free air, and needs a woman of reproductive age.
why.D: Pancreatitis does not produce pneumoperitoneum.

stem: A 55-year-old man is brought to the ER with profuse vomiting of large amounts of bright red blood over 4 hours. His blood pressure is 70/40 mmHg and pulse is 120/min. He dies 1 hour after admission despite resuscitation efforts. Autopsy shows a deep peptic ulcer localized proximally on the lesser curvature of the stomach. The ulcer most likely penetrated which of the following arteries?
expl: An ulcer high (proximal) on the lesser curvature erodes the left gastric artery, which runs along the lesser curve. A posterior duodenal bulb ulcer erodes the gastroduodenal artery.

why.A: The SMA supplies the midgut; it doesn't run along the stomach.
why.B: The common hepatic artery runs above the pancreas, not in the lesser curve wall.
why.C: The right gastroepiploic artery runs along the greater curvature.
why.D: Correct — left gastric artery (proximal lesser curvature).

stem: A 60-year-old man with a history of peptic ulcer disease presents with melena and hematemesis. He is hypotensive and has a hemoglobin of 8.2 g/dL. Nasogastric lavage returns fresh blood. He has been initially resuscitated with IV fluids and blood transfusion. What is the next step in management?

opts.t: IV PPI and endoscopy within 24 hours

expl: After resuscitation of a bleeding ulcer, start an IV PPI and perform endoscopy within 24 hours (diagnostic and therapeutic — injection, coagulation, clips). Surgery or embolization only if endoscopy fails.

why.A: Surgery is for failure of endoscopic haemostasis.
why.C: Oral PPI is for after haemostasis or minor bleeds.
why.D: CT angiography/embolization is the next step if endoscopic therapy fails (or the source can't be found).

stem: The left gastric artery arises from which of the following major arteries?
expl: The coeliac trunk has three branches: left gastric, common hepatic and splenic.

why.A: Correct.
why.B: The SMA supplies the midgut (gives the inferior pancreaticoduodenal, jejunal/ileal, middle colic…).
why.C: The IMA supplies the hindgut.
why.D: The left gastric is a branch of the coeliac trunk, not the aorta directly.

stem: A 38-year-old man presents with recurrent peptic ulcers that have not responded to proton pump inhibitor therapy. Fasting gastrin levels are found to be markedly elevated. He also reports occasional diarrhea and abdominal discomfort. What is the most likely diagnosis?
srcNote: (Stomach and Duodenum) Source note (Final 442 F Q3): In the related refractory-ulcer recall, the original key is Answer: A; option A is Neuroendocrine tumor.
expl: Recurrent ulcers refractory to PPIs + markedly raised fasting gastrin + diarrhoea (acid inactivates pancreatic enzymes) = Zollinger–Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma). The related recall keyed "neuroendocrine tumour" — a gastrinoma is a neuroendocrine tumour.

why.A: Correct.
why.B: H. pylori ulcers respond to therapy and gastrin is not markedly raised.
why.C: NSAID ulcers heal once NSAIDs stop; gastrin is normal.
why.D: Gastric cancer doesn't produce gastrin or refractory multiple ulcers.

stem: A 42-year-old man presents with epigastric pain that worsens on an empty stomach. Endoscopy reveals an anterior duodenal ulcer, and testing is positive for H. pylori. What is the most appropriate treatment?

opts.t: Triple therapy for H. pylori eradication
Surgical ulcer due to perforation risk

expl: An uncomplicated H. pylori-positive duodenal ulcer is treated by eradicating H. pylori (PPI + clarithromycin + amoxicillin, or quadruple therapy) — this heals the ulcer and prevents recurrence.

why.A: Correct — eradication therapy.
why.B: PPI alone heals the ulcer, but it recurs if H. pylori isn't eradicated.
why.C: An anterior ulcer can perforate, but an uncomplicated ulcer is not operated on.
why.D: Vagotomy is a historical operation for refractory ulcers; PUD is now treated medically.

stem: A patient who uses NSAIDs came with a perforated ulcer. What to do?
expl: A perforated peptic ulcer is closed with an omental (Graham) patch — open or laparoscopic — plus washout; then stop NSAIDs, PPI, and treat H. pylori.

why.A: Correct.
why.C: Roux-en-Y is a bypass/reconstruction, not emergency ulcer repair.
why.D: Nissen fundoplication is for GERD/hiatus hernia.

stem: Patient done Roux-e-Y procedure and after a while presented with symptoms of marginal ulcer what’s the most common cause of that?
expl: Marginal ulcers at the gastrojejunal anastomosis after Roux-en-Y bypass are mostly caused by NSAIDs (and smoking) — patients are told to avoid NSAIDs for life.

why.A: Acetaminophen is the safe analgesic after bypass.
why.C: Warfarin increases bleeding but doesn't cause ulcers.
why.D: Hydroxyurea is not linked to marginal ulcers.

stem: A young patient with a duodenal ulcer presents with bleeding. Endoscopy with dual modality was performed, but the patient continues to bleed and is now unstable. What is the next step in management?

opts.t: Laparotomy with duodenotomy and ulcer oversewing

srcNote: The check mark is reproduced from the source; no separate answer key is provided. Only three options are supplied in the source.
expl: Bleeding that continues after endoscopic dual therapy in an unstable patient → surgery: laparotomy, duodenotomy and under-running (oversewing) of the bleeding ulcer (ligating the gastroduodenal artery). Angioembolization is an option in a stable patient where available.

why.A: Repeating endoscopy (YAG laser) is unsafe in an unstable patient after endoscopic failure.
why.B: Angioembolization needs time and stability; the unstable patient goes to theatre.
why.C: Correct — the source's checked answer.

stem: A patient with a persistent duodenal ulcer now presents with vomiting of undigested food, indicating pyloric obstruction. What is the appropriate management?
srcNote: The check mark is reproduced from the source; no separate answer key is provided.
expl: Pyloric (gastric outlet) obstruction from chronic duodenal ulcer scarring → NG decompression, correct fluids/electrolytes (hypokalaemic hypochloraemic alkalosis), EGD to exclude malignancy, then surgery (resection or bypass) — the source's checked answer. Endoscopic balloon dilatation is an alternative in selected patients.

why.A: Balloon dilation can be tried, but fibrotic chronic stenosis often recurs; the keyed answer is decompression then surgery.
why.C: Eradication alone doesn't open a fixed scar.
why.D: PPI alone doesn't open a fixed scar.

stem: What is the most common site of gastrinoma (excluding the pancreas)?
srcNote: The check mark is reproduced from the source; no separate answer key is provided.
expl: Most gastrinomas lie in the "gastrinoma triangle"; outside the pancreas the duodenum is the commonest site (in MEN 1 they are mostly duodenal).

why.A: The bile duct is a rare site.
why.C: The stomach is not a common site.
why.D: The liver is where metastases go, not the primary site.

stem: After Billroth II surgery for a duodenal ulcer, the patient develops fever and tachycardia. What is the most likely cause?
ansText: Duodenal stump leak — the blind duodenal stump of a Billroth II can blow out (usually days 2–7), causing peritonitis/sepsis (fever, tachycardia, pain).

stem: A patient has ulcer symptoms, and endoscopy shows diffuse ulceration throughout the stomach. What is the most likely cause?
ansText: NSAIDs — they cause multiple diffuse erosions/ulcers by blocking prostaglandin protection (the source gave the answer without options).

stem: A forty-year-old male taking low dose aspirin is brought to ER with sudden onset of severe epigastric pain. He is a known case of duodenal ulcer. On examination he is tachycardic with pulse of 125/min, normotensive. Examination of his abdomen reveals tenderness and guarding over all quadrants What is the most appropriate investigation?
expl: Sudden severe epigastric pain in a known DU patient on aspirin, with tachycardia and generalized guarding = perforation until proven otherwise → erect chest X-ray to look for free air under the diaphragm.

why.A: Never do endoscopy in suspected perforation (insufflation worsens the leak).
why.B: A barium enema looks at the colon; barium in the peritoneum is dangerous.
why.C: Amylase can rise mildly in perforation; it doesn't confirm it.
why.D: Correct — erect CXR.

stem: What is the best non-invasive test to confirm h.pylori eradication ?
expl: Urea breath test is the best non-invasive test to confirm eradication (stool antigen is an alternative). Stop PPIs 2 weeks and antibiotics 4 weeks before testing.

why.A: Correct.
why.C: Serology stays positive after eradication — it can't show cure.
why.D: Stool antigen is acceptable, but the breath test is the classic best answer.

stem: Patient in ICU bleeds from NGT, he was intubated >48 hrs and on vasopressors. Ordered for him EGD (esophagogastroduodenoscopy). What should be done to prevent this complication?
expl: Ventilation >48 h and coagulopathy/shock are indications for stress-ulcer prophylaxis with acid suppression (PPI/H2 blocker).

why.A: Correct.
why.B: Enteral feeding actually protects the mucosa.
why.C: Not indicated.
why.D: Used for variceal prophylaxis, not stress ulcers.

stem: A 50 y/o man, who is known to have peptic ulcer disease is brought to the hospital with a history of vomiting bright red blood 3 times at home. On initial examination, he produced incomprehensible sounds, opened his eyes on painful stimuli and was able to localize painful stimuli. His pulse is 120 bpm, BP 85/60 mmHg. O2 saturation is 93% on room air. Which one of the following is the most appropriate 1st step in the management of this patient?
expl: GCS ~9 (E2V2M5) with hematemesis → the airway is at risk → airway control first.

why.A: Correct.
why.C: Bridge for varices.
why.D: Not resuscitation.

stem: Which of the following is the most common cause of upper GI bleeding?
expl: Peptic ulcer is the commonest cause of upper GI bleeding (~45% on the slide).

why.A: Angiodysplasia is a lower GI bleeding cause.
why.C: Varices are ~20% — common in cirrhotics but second to peptic ulcer.
why.D: Correct.

stem: Which of the following ulcers are at high risk of rebleeding?
srcNote: ( skin , soft tissue and wound management) 438A
expl: Endoscopic stigmata, from highest rebleeding risk: active bleeding > non-bleeding visible vessel > adherent clot > flat pigmented spot > clean base. Of the options given, an adherent clot carries the highest risk.

why.A: A scarring/healing ulcer is low risk.
why.C: A clean/visible base without a vessel is low risk.
why.D: Multiple erosions are superficial and rarely rebleed seriously.

stem: A 50 year old male patient presented to the hospital with a history of melena. He was previously fit and healthy without any medical illness. A digital rectal examination confirmed the presence of melena. His BP was 110/70 mmHg, pulse 90/min and hemoglobin of 10 g/dl. When you do risk stratification for upper GI bleeding, the patient lays in which of the following categories?
expl: Same recall as Midterm 432: age < 60, pulse < 100, SBP > 100, no comorbidity → pre-endoscopic Rockall score 0 → low risk.

why.A: Not a standard category.
why.C: Needs shock, age or comorbidity.
why.D: Needs shock/major comorbidity.

stem: 20 years old college student smoke 20 cigarettes a day presented with epigastric pain, you suspected duodenal ulcer. What’s the appropriate next management to confirm diagnosis?
expl: The test that confirms a duodenal ulcer is upper GI endoscopy — it sees the ulcer, allows biopsy/CLO test and can treat bleeding.

why.A: Plain X-ray only shows complications (free air).
why.B: The breath test shows H. pylori, not the ulcer itself.
why.C: Correct.
why.D: Barium studies are less sensitive and can't biopsy.

stem: which of the ulcer are at risk of re bleeding:
srcNote: . Source note (Midterm 432 F Q21): (Davidson page 190. 431 surgery booklet page 62). Stigmata of rebleeding in order from the highest risk is as the following: 1- Active bleeding, 2- Non-bleeding visible vessel, 3- Adherent clot, 4- Flat pigment spot, 5- Clean base
expl: Rebleeding risk order: active bleeding > non-bleeding visible vessel (~50%) > adherent clot (~30%) > flat pigmented spot (~10%) > clean base (< 5%). The highest among these is the visible vessel.

why.A: Clean base — lowest risk.
why.C: Correct — visible vessel.
why.D: Adherent clot — intermediate risk (below a visible vessel).

stem: 48 y\o man known to have chronic prepyloric peptic ulcer, presented to ER with a history of frequent vomiting since 4 days. On examination he was dehydrated. Upper GI endoscopy showed gastric outlet obstruction. Which of the following acid-base balance this patient may have?
srcNote: (Principles of Fluids and Electrolytes Balance in Surgical Patients) Source note (Midterm 429 F Q38): Peptic ulcer disease causes gastric outlet obstruction, causing a metabolic derangement hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis.
expl: Gastric outlet obstruction → loss of HCl → metabolic alkalosis with hypokalemia.

why.A: No.
why.C: No.
why.D: No.

stem: A patient has signs and symptoms of perforation, and imaging already shows air under the diaphragm. What would you do next?
srcNote: ?? Missing choices you already know there is air under diaphragm through imaging why would you order erect x-ray again? This recall has three blank options and no confirmed answer. The original uncertainty is retained above.
ansText: No further imaging (a repeat erect X-ray adds nothing) — resuscitate (ABC, NPO, IV fluids, NGT, Foley, antibiotics, PPI, analgesia) and proceed to urgent surgical repair (Graham omental patch). The source had no options or answer.

stem: patient with perforation of proximal duodenum it was in the emergency setting, what surgery would you do next?
expl: In the emergency setting a perforated duodenal ulcer is closed with a simple omental (Graham) patch. Definitive acid-reducing operations aren't done now — PPI and H. pylori eradication follow.

why.A: Highly selective vagotomy is an elective acid-reducing operation, not an emergency one.
why.B: Antrectomy + vagotomy is too big an operation in an emergency.
why.C: Truncal vagotomy is unnecessary now that PPIs and eradication work.
why.D: Correct.

stem: A 50- year old male presented to the hospital with history of melena. He’s previously fit and healthy without any medical illness. A digital rectal examination confirms presence of melena. His blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg, pulse 90/minute and hemoglobin is 10/dl. When you do risk stratification for upper GI bleeding, this patient falls in which of the following categories?
expl: Risk scores for upper GI bleeding (Rockall pre-endoscopy): age < 60 = 0, no shock (pulse < 100, SBP > 100) = 0, no comorbidity = 0 → score 0 = low risk. He is haemodynamically stable with mild anaemia → low risk.

why.A: "Very low" isn't a standard Rockall category.
why.C: Moderate risk needs shock, older age or comorbidity.
why.D: High risk = shock, major comorbidity, active bleeding.

stem: A 45 y/o patient admitted to burn unit 3 weeks ago with 40% full thickness burn referred surgery with history of vomiting large amount of fresh blood.Which of the following is the most likely source of the bleeding?
srcNote: ( Burns ) Curling's ulcer is an acute gastric erosion resulting as a complication from severe burns when reduced plasma volume leads to ischemia and cell necrosis (sloughing) of the gastric mucosa.
expl: Curling's ulcer = acute stress ulceration of the stomach/duodenum after major burns (hypovolaemia → mucosal ischaemia). Prevent with early enteral feeding and acid suppression.

why.A: Gastric varices need portal hypertension.
why.C: Correct — burns → Curling's.
why.D: Cushing's ulcer follows head/CNS injury (vagal overstimulation → high acid).

stem: A 25-year-old patient presented to the emergency department with a history of vomiting blood and passing dark stool for 1 day after receiving Non-steroidal antiinflammatory drugs for his knee injury 3 weeks ago. Which ONE of the following is the most likely cause of his bleeding?
expl: Haematemesis and melena in a young man after NSAIDs for a knee injury → NSAID-induced peptic ulcer (NSAIDs block prostaglandins that protect the mucosa).

why.A: Nothing suggests coagulopathy.
why.B: A healthy 25-year-old has no portal hypertension.
why.C: Mallory–Weiss needs forceful vomiting first.
why.D: Correct.

stem: Young male came with Upper GI Bleeding in endoscopy he found to have peptic ulcer and breath test prove Helicobacter pylori which one of the Following will not be in your management plan?
expl: Somatostatin/octreotide lowers portal pressure — it is used for variceal bleeding, not for a bleeding peptic ulcer. Ulcer bleeding: ABC, hospital observation, PPI, endoscopic therapy, H. pylori eradication.

why.A: Always part of the plan.
why.B: Admission and observation are needed after a bleed.
why.C: Correct — not part of ulcer management.
why.D: A PPI is essential.
